ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: world events
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Rare happenings across the region that last a while: a plague, a famine, a warlord's rise, a chief's death, a new town.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: When the neighbors have a hard year, what you send them is remembered.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
Rimfolk events happen to the colony. World events happen to the whole region around it, and last: a plague among the neighbors, a famine, a warlord rising among a hostile people, a chief's death and the quarrel over the seat, a town founded or abandoned, a great fair. Each lasts from about a week to a month, changes what the colony meets while it lasts, puts a few questions to the council along the way, and ends in a way that depends on what the colony did.
They come on Rimfolk's own slow rhythm, apart from the storyteller: about one every 30 to 60 days (the setting is the average, 45 days by default, and it varies by a third either way). At most two run at the same time, never two of one kind, and a new one waits while a fight is going on at home or a world event's question is still unanswered. Each one also waits a long while before it can come again.

li.heading: Reading one
li.text:
The first letter says what is happening, where, and to whom, and ends with what it means for the colony and about how long it may last. The council window's World page shows each running world event at the top, under "In the world": the people at the heart of it, what it means for the colony, what the colony has done so far, and a bar for the time it may still last. Hover over it for what it makes likelier or rarer. It can end sooner than the bar says: a warlord can fall tomorrow.
While it lasts, Rimfolk events that fit it come more or less often, and so do some of the game's own: more herds in a migration, more cold snaps in a hard winter, plague likelier in a plague year, fewer caravans on a bandit road. The game's own only change with the deeper game hooks on, and only where your storyteller picks among a kind of event by weight; some storytellers send traders on a fixed rhythm whatever the weights say. The arrivals a world event sends itself (a new town's first traders, pilgrims, a herd) come either way.

li.heading: The world events

table.li: World event | While it lasts | The colony's part
A warlord rises | His people raid harder and more often, and he leads some raids | Pay him off, post a bounty, help his hunters, ask an ally to march, wait him out, or bring him down at home
Plague in the region | Fewer caravans and visitors, refugees, sickness likelier at home | Medicine for the sick, shelter for refugees, the colony's doctor's advice
Famine | Hungry pilgrims and travelers, now and then a desperate raid | Food at a gift, a fair price or famine prices, shelter for the hungry
Hard winter | Cold snaps, fewer traders, travelers caught by the snow | Firewood for the neighbors, a roof for the snowbound
Locust swarm | The swarm may strip the open fields; a famine can follow | Smudge fires, an early harvest, or both
Flood downriver (by a river) | Refugees, things washed up on the bank | Shelter, and timber to rebuild
A new leader | The new leader's nature (kind, greedy, harsh or steady) changes trade and goodwill | A gift or a few words for the funeral
A contested seat | Two claimants fight over a neighbor's seat | Back one, or stay out of it
A war of words (Ideology) | Two neighbors' creeds quarrel in public | Speak for one, host a debate, or stay out
Peace talks | Two neighbors at war ask the colony to host talks | Host them, and maybe end their war for good
Sellswords | A mercenary company looks for work | Hire them against a hostile people, feed them, or send them on
Bandit road | Fewer caravans and visitors, merchants stranded, a bandit raid now and then | Pay for guards, look after the robbed
A new town | A real new settlement nearby, its first traders, more caravans | A welcome gift, or timber to sell
A town abandoned | Families leaving; the town is gone when it ends | Shelter, and what's left behind
A trading season | Many more caravans and merchants' offers | A toll, or a rest stop for traders
A great fair | More visitors and traders, music and contests | A cart of surplus to sell, an entry in a contest
A great pilgrimage | Many more pilgrims and travelers | A camp for the pilgrims, free or for a fee
A silver rush | Prospectors and travelers; some want to stay | Let them dig for a share or a fee
A famous healer | A healer tours the region | Invite them to mend a colonist's worst lasting condition
The great herds | Herds and rare beasts pass far more often | Let the neighbors' hunters across, or charge them
Strange herds (Alpha Animals) | Strange creatures and herds pass far more often | A skilled handler may win one over
A season of wild magic (A RimWorld of Magic) | Shards fall from the sky more often | Let a mage study the surge

A long drought upriver | Heat waves likelier, fewer caravans, thirsty herders and hungry travelers; a famine may follow | Water for their herds, a builder for a new well, food at a gift or a fair price
A new road | Travelers, visitors and stranded carts more often; traders come more often once it opens | Timber for the road, a builder for a day, a say in where it runs
A holy year | Many more pilgrims and travelers, fewer fights | Feed the pilgrims, forgive a neighbor's debt, let a colonist keep a vow
A bandit lord falls | Deserters, wounded strangers and buried loot from the broken band; a lieutenant may gather the rest | Shelter for stragglers, a treasure map, a cart for the victory feast
Sickness in the herds | Animal sickness likelier at home unless the colony pens its animals, fewer caravans | Pen the animals, lend a handler, food for the neighbors

A ship comes down (industrial and later) | Ship chunks, pods and survivors more often, cheap steel and components; scavengers may raid | Buy salvage, take in survivors, let a colonist look over the wreck
The Empire's levy (Royalty) | The Empire asks its neighbors for silver for a far campaign | Pay in full and be named in the dispatches, pay half, or decline

Deserters on the roads (Vanilla Factions Expanded - Empire) | Imperial patrols hunt deserters; one asks the colony for shelter | Take them in, hand them over for the reward, or feed them and send them on
The republic votes (Vanilla Factions Expanded - Classical) | A republic elects its consuls, old families against reformers | Back a side with silver, or stay out of it
Gold fever (Vanilla Factions Expanded - Settlers) | Prospectors on every road, more travelers and traders | Let a prospector work the stream for a share
A great fire | A neighbor's town burns; burned-out families on the roads | Timber for the roofs, shelter for a family, a builder to raise the roofs
A blood feud | Two families of two friendly peoples at each other's throats | Hide the young man who ran, or hand him over; a good talker between the families; the last of the blood price
A comet | Fortune tellers, pilgrims and scholars come more often | A night watch on the hill, a stargazer on it, a fragment fetched from the hills
A bumper harvest (summer, fall) | More traders, cheap grain, harvest missions likelier | Buy grain cheap, send hands for their harvest, hold a harvest supper
The drove roads | Drovers camp more often, strays wander in | Grazing for a fee or as friends, a drovers' quarrel to judge
A people in mourning | Mourners on the roads and at the colony's gate | Silver for the stone or words for the wake; stand by the road as the dead go by
A season of songs | Minstrels and players come more often; a song about the colony goes round | A gift for the next verse, a supper and a bed for the singer
A toll on the roads (medieval and later) | Far fewer caravans unless the colony pays its way | Pay the toll, or join the villages' petition against it
Iron gone scarce (medieval and later) | Smiths and tinkers come more often | Steel at twice its worth or its plain worth, a crafter to teach their smiths
Exiles on the roads | A neighbor casts out a household; exiles ask for shelter | Take them in against the neighbor's wishes, feed them and send them on, or turn them away; later, speak for them
Rebuilding (follows a war, a fire or a flood) | The people it hit rebuild; their homeless pass the colony on the way back | Timber, a builder for the bridge, food for the families going home

The road reopens (follows a bandit road, a hard winter, a flood, a plague, a toll, a war, a drought or closed markets) | Many more caravans and visitors for a while | Trade with the first caravan, a standing order of meals, a stop for caravans at the colony's well

A prophet on the roads | Pilgrims and camps come more often; her followers pass on the road | Bread for her followers or a night by the wall, her words at the gate at dusk, an answer for the neighbor's ruler who wants them home
An old vault opened | Scholars, camps and caravans come more often | A reader for the old writing, a scavenger's crates bought unseen, advice on the deeper door

Markets closed | One neighbor shuts out another's traders, who come round by the colony's road | Cheap cloth from the shut-out people, a smuggler's cart hidden or reported, a side taken, a talker between them
A merchant house fails | Fewer caravans, more wanderers | The house's pemmican cheap, an unpaid driver taken on, a loan to its old master, a search in the hills for its last wagon

The ice road (winter, in a hard freeze) | Many more caravans and travelers over the frozen lakes | Wood for the poles, a driver pulled out of the ice, hot meals for a caravan, fires on the shore at the thaw
A moot of the peoples | More visitors and travelers | A speaker and a gift for the host's table, supper for the delegates, a vote on two neighbors' pastures
An old thrumbo (spring to fall, where one could pass) | Thrumbos pass far more often | Let the horn hunters through for a share or turn them away, a dawn walk to see it, a turn at its watch

li.after: Questions come with a deadline, like Rimfolk events, and an unanswered one falls to its default, which is usually doing nothing. Some world events can lead to another when they end: a drought or sickness in the herds that nobody eased can turn into a famine, a new road into a trading season, a bandit lord's fall into a warlord's rise or a company of sellswords looking for work. Two come only after another has ended, with that one's people: rebuilding after a war, a fire or a flood, and the road reopening once the bandits, the snow, the water, the sickness, the toll or a closed market are gone.

li.heading: Answers that come back
li.text:
Some beats only come because of an earlier answer in the same world event, so the same one plays differently from game to game. In a plague, the neighbors' doctors may ask the colony to shut its gate to travelers: while it holds, caravans, visitors and wanderers come far less often, and so do plague and flu. Feed a prophet's followers and two of them come back with healroot; hide the boy from a blood feud and his mother comes to the gate with her weaving; send timber after a great fire and the town's carter brings the first boards from its new mill; graze the drovers' herd as friends and they leave a young beast on the way home; stand by the road for a neighbor's dead and the family sends a keepsake. Open the old lane across the colony's land to a carter dodging a toll and caravans come more often, unless the tollmen find it.
A loan to a failing merchant house is paid back when the world event ends: a third over if the house is saved, which happens about 9 times in 10 if the colony searched the hills for its lost wagon and half the time if not, and just under half of it if the house is wound up. Horn hunters let through after an old thrumbo bring the colony's share only if they get the horn.

li.heading: The warlord
li.text:
While he rises, his people's raids hit 20% harder, and about 3 in 10 of the raids the storyteller would have sent from someone else come from his people instead. He walks in with about 4 in 10 of their raids, and his band attacks the colony on its own every 8 to 12 days, up to three times, at about the storyteller's usual strength. Those fights only come with battles in Rimfolk events switched on.
None of it needs the colony to storm his town. The peoples at war with his hunt him, and from the fifth day the chance that they bring him down grows every day, faster the more towns they have against his. A bounty adds 3% a day and brings bounty hunters too; silver sent to his hunters adds 1.5% a day each time. An ally of the colony at war with his people can be asked to march: it costs 20 goodwill with them, and they win between 3 and 8 times in 10, depending on their towns and arms against his. A truce bought with silver stops his band's raids, but 3 times in 10 he breaks it within about a week. And after half his time is up, a band that gets nothing breaks up, 2% a day, 4% more for every raid of his people the colony has beaten off.
Killed at home, he's finished, and whoever struck the blow and anyone his raiders hurt feel it. Taken alive, the council chooses: keep him, hand him to his enemies for trial (15 goodwill with them), or let his people ransom him. If he simply rides away, the colonists his raiders hurt won't like it.

li.heading: The region remembers
li.text:
Most world events keep count of what the colony gave: medicine, food, firewood, shelter, a gift, a word in the right place. Endings pay that off, usually with goodwill on top of what each answer gave (10 more with the people the colony stood by in a plague or a famine). A people the colony helped through a hard year is remembered as helped from then on: the letters say so when their next hard year comes, and a famous healer from among them asks half the usual price.
Not every answer is kind, and that's remembered too. Famine prices fill the stores with silver and cost goodwill when the hungry year ends. Backing the losing claimant for a seat costs more than staying out of it. Goodwill lost to a world event stops short of turning a people hostile; only the colony's own choices start wars.
The people the colony stood by keep it in their memory for years, with what the colony did for them and against them besides (see what the world remembers): old friends may send food or medicine when the colony's own hard year comes, and refugees from a world event may ask to be seen through.

li.heading: What follows
li.text:
Some days or weeks after a world event ends, its people may come back about it, once for each world event, depending on how it ended. After a plague the colony helped with, its survivors come to give thanks (accept the gift, say their dead's names with them, or tell them to keep it). After a famine the colony helped with, the first harvest is shared. After a flood, the people of the drowned town come up the river looking for what the water took, and the colony may have it in the barn. After a hard winter in which the colony sheltered the snowbound, they come back in spring with seed and offer to help plant it. After locusts, a famine or a drought, old friends of the colony (a people that remembers its good turns) send seed grain. And after a plague, a famine, a flood, a hard winter or a great fire the colony looked away from, an elder of the people comes to say, very calmly, what it cost them.
Refugees to see through come not only while a plague, a famine, a flood, a hard winter, a fire or a war runs, but for some weeks after it has ended too. What a people remembers of the colony colours the letters of world events about them: an old friend's first rider asks for the colonist they remember by name.

li.heading: What you'll see
li.text: With "Answers play out on the map" on, what a world event's answer sends really goes out. Medicine, food, firewood or silver for the rider is carried out of the stores to the gate, where the rider or the cart waits, and only then is it gone; a work party brings the harvest in early before the locusts come, and a few keep watch over the smudge fires in the fields by night. The goodwill and the moods come as always; the moods wait for those who went. Answers on the map says how it works.

li.heading: The world map
li.text: Some world events change the world for good. A new town is a real settlement, founded a few days' travel from the colony on open land, and it stays. An abandoned town is gone from the map when the world event ends, with an abandoned settlement in its place, unless the colony has a caravan on its way there or a quest about it then; in that case a few families stay on and the town remains. A neighbor's new leader is the one the game itself chooses. Peace made at the colony's table is real peace between the two peoples. With Factional War running, which has wars and peace of its own, peace talks never come.

li.heading: Other settlers
li.text: Once the colony is well established, a party of settlers of a friendly people may found a steading a few days off: a new town on the world map, with a leader who walks up to the colony's gate in the first days to say hello and ask for timber. This is the longest world event, nearly a year, and it runs in stages: their hunters work the colony's woods (let them, divide the hunting grounds with them, or warn them off); a hungry month when their first planting fails and they ask for food (or, if the colony has slighted them, their traps turn up on the colony's side of the stream and a marked beast goes home over their shoulders); word of the steading's growth, household by household, shown on the World page; and at the turning of the year the leader comes back in person. Every warm answer (a gift, trade, shared hunting, food given or sold, a quarrel settled) is weighed against every slight (a cold word, a warning off, food refused, their traps pulled up): the settlers are sour on the colony when the slights are as many as the warm answers. To a colony they are warm to, the leader offers an alliance, or to join the colony outright, if the steading is still small enough (five households at most); to one they are sour on, a boundary to agree or nothing at all. The year ends one of six ways: allies (goodwill, their traders come first), the settlers come over and the steading is left empty, bad blood (goodwill lost, a scuffle at the stream that hurts nobody badly), the settlers give up and go home (an abandoned settlement is left), or plain neighbours, helped or not. Allies answer in a bad year: when the colony's stores fall under six days of food they send two of theirs with sacks of their harvest, and when the colony is attacked their fighters come first (see "camps", the war party).

li.heading: The road, over a year
li.text: "A new road" is the start of a longer story when the colony has the surveyors run it past the gate. Weeks after it opens, the road comes into use: merchants turn in to trade, travelers rest by it, a carter robbed on it walks up in his stockings (a meal and a bed, silver for the road, or nothing), and the people's road wardens stop to water their horses. Make the wardens welcome and, some weeks later, they ask for ground for a post by the colony: let them build on the colony's land and their camp comes to put it up, and when it stands (about a week) it settles as the colony's neighbour, like a camp let stay for good (see "camps"), keeping the road and riding out against whatever comes up it. Or the post goes up a day down the road, or not at all. Where the post was kept, a crossroads town grows up at it a season or two later, a new town on the world map with a market every week, and the people's reeve asks whether the town may take the colony's name. Each of these world events follows the one before, once, so the road's story takes a year or two of game time, and it stops wherever the colony's answers stop it.

li.heading: People a world event leaves behind
li.text: Hardships in the region put people on the road to the colony. In a plague, besides the family looking for shelter, an old woman may bring two children orphaned by the sickness to the gate: take the children in (she goes home alone in the morning), send them on with food toward the people's elders, or turn them away. In a famine the hungry family and the orphan girl come as before, and refugee camps come three times as often. A war, a holy war, a levy or a mercenary company in the news brings deserters: a handful of a friendly people's fighters who camp out of sight at the edge of the colony's land, asking only to rest a few days and not be spoken of. They ask for a little steel to mend their gear, can be hired or paid silver for the road, and can be asked to stand guard: from then on they take up arms against whatever threatens the colony while their camp stands, as a war party does. Some of them ask to stay.
